author: dev
title: Add retry settings for the delivery worker

explain.what: The Billing API key is written directly in config.py.
explain.why: Everyone who can read the repository can now read the key. Deleting the line later does not help: the code history keeps every old version forever.
explain.realWorld: Leaked keys in source code are one of the most common causes of security incidents. The fix is never just "delete it": the key must be replaced with a new one ("rotated") and loaded from a secrets manager.
explain.tell: Look for long random-looking strings next to words like KEY, TOKEN, SECRET or PASSWORD.

explain.why: You had to guess why the retry limit went from 3 to 5. Was there an outage? A customer complaint? A reviewer who does not know the reason cannot judge whether the change is right.
explain.realWorld: Teams often ask for the description first and review second. Two sentences from the author save every later reader the same guesswork.
explain.tell: Read the description before the code. If it is empty or just repeats the title, say so.

hints.look: You do not need to understand the code for this one. Is there anything in this file that should not be visible to everyone who can open it?
hints.region: Look closely at the lines around the Billing settings.
hints.reveal: The line that sets BILLING_API_KEY contains a real key, in plain text. Click that line and mark it as "Secret in the code".

author: priya
title: Look up the price from Billing before delivery
description: Fetches the per-message price so we can attach it to the delivery receipt.

explain.what: The call to Billing has no timeout.
explain.why: If Billing becomes slow or stops answering, this line waits forever. Every delivery now waits behind it, so a problem in Billing becomes an outage in Queue Service.
explain.realWorld: This is how one slow service takes down the services that depend on it. Amazon's public engineering guidance is to set a timeout on every call to another service.
explain.tell: Whenever code talks to something over the network, ask: what happens if the other side never answers?

explain.what: The CR adds a new function and changes deliver(), with no tests.
explain.why: Nothing checks that the price ends up on the receipt, or what happens when Billing returns an error. The next person to edit this file can break it without noticing.
explain.realWorld: Reviewers are expected to check for tests, not just read the logic. Untested code tends to break later, when its author has moved on.
explain.tell: New behavior with no new test lines in the diff.

hints.region: Read the new fetch_price function line by line.

author: dev
title: Page through a customer's queued messages
description: Adds a helper for the console's message list. Returns one page at a time. Includes a test.

explain.what: Each page is one item short. A page size of 20 returns 19 messages.
explain.why: In Python, messages[start:end] already stops before `end`. Subtracting 1 again drops the last message of every page, so customers never see it.
explain.realWorld: The included test passes, because it only checks the first item. A test that passes is not proof that the code is right: check what the test actually asserts.
explain.tell: Any time you see +1 or -1 near a range, work through a tiny example by hand. Page size 2 from [a, b, c, d]: do you get [a, b]?

explain.what: The customer's name and email address are written to the log.
explain.why: Logs are copied to many systems and read by many people. Personal data in logs is a privacy problem and, in many countries, a legal one.
explain.realWorld: Companies have paid large fines for this. The usual fix is to log an internal ID, which means nothing to an outsider, instead of the name or email.
explain.tell: Read every log line and ask: would I be comfortable if this were printed on a screen in the hallway?

hints.look: Two things here. First: try the paging by hand with a small list. Second: read what gets written to the log.
hints.region: Work through get_page with page 1 and page size 2 on [a, b, c, d]. How many items come back?
hints.reveal: `end = start + page_size - 1` makes every page one item short: mark it "Off by one". And the logger.info line records the customer's name and email: mark it "Personal data in logs".

author: priya
title: small fix: keep retrying failed deliveries
description: Deliveries were being dropped when the receiver was briefly down. Now we keep trying until it works.

explain.what: The loop retries forever, with no limit and no pause between tries.
explain.why: If the receiver is down, every worker hammers it as fast as it can. When it tries to come back up, the flood of retries knocks it down again. And one bad message blocks the worker for good.
explain.realWorld: This pattern is called a retry storm, and it turns small outages into long ones. The standard practice is a limited number of retries, with a longer wait each time ("backoff") and a little randomness so clients do not all retry at the same instant.
explain.tell: `while True` around a network call. Ask: when does this stop, and how fast does it spin?

explain.what: `except Exception: pass` hides every error, not just delivery failures.
explain.why: A typo, a missing value, a full disk: all of them now vanish without a trace. The worker looks busy while doing nothing, and no alarm will ever fire.
explain.realWorld: Silent failures are the hardest to debug because there is nothing to look at. The old code caught only DeliveryError and raised DeliveryFailed in the end, which is what made the problem visible.
explain.tell: `except` followed by `pass`, or catching the broadest possible error type.

hints.look: The title says "small fix". Compare what the old code did when delivery kept failing with what the new code does.
hints.region: Read the new loop. When does it stop? What happens to an error?
hints.reveal: `while True` never gives up and never waits: mark it "Retries forever". And `except Exception: pass` throws away every error: mark it "Error is hidden".

plain.5: Deliver one message, trying again if it fails.
plain.6: Old code: try a limited number of times.
plain.8: Old code: send the message. If it works, we are done.
plain.9: Old code: if delivery specifically failed…
plain.10: …wait a while (longer each time) before the next try.
plain.11: Old code: after the last try, give up loudly so someone finds out.
plain.14: New code: send the message. If it works, we are done.
plain.15: New code: if anything at all goes wrong…
plain.16: …do nothing, and go round the loop again immediately.
